title: WebMCP

As you guys can see, first, I just do my job once. I created a customer. I created a customer and I bill an invoice. That's it. No coding, no scripts. Deputy watches these steps as demonstration. Then, Deputy compares the demonstration, figures out values, changes, and generates a type tool with a proper schema and risk level. I approve it and register for agents to use. The human authored a capability just by working. Now a agent tries to use a risky tool, a refund, watches what happens. title: Living Evidence Demo — Scientific Documents Agents Can Cross-Examine

They come directly from the page, no table scraping, and no copied notebook. I'll ask the agent to inspect the manifest and evaluate the headline claim. The page runs its own deterministic analysis, renders the result back into our shared view, and records the action. The famous claim loses. Rule failed. That does not mean false. It means this author registered rule did not pass on the current evidence. The manifest also says 19 effect size records represent 18 experiments with zero primary reports checked. Now I can compose a sensitivity question the author never had to pre-build as a button. The agent calls a bounded rerun. The page draws a new forest plot, and the SHA-256 ledger keeps the exact inputs and result digest. The page refuses to turn reproducibility into certainty. Provenance gaps and risk of bias are explicit. The PDF versus web MCP benchmark starts at zero runs, so we make no speed or accuracy claim. On the authoring side, agents can propose but cannot approve. Every row needs a source, locator, quote, derivation, design, estimate, and explicit risk of bias status. Only this human click admits it. Approval accepts an extraction. It does not verify it. The new evidence board generalizes the idea beyond meta-analysis. title: Agentdesk
transcript: AI agents can operate websites, but giving them every available tool creates confusion, risk, and unnecessary context. Agent desk turns web MCP capabilities into governed workflows. So like a good human being, I'm going to thank my AI and then I'm going to exit. Thanks a lot, ChatGPT. >> Anytime. Happy to help. >> Thank you so much for watching. I hope you enjoyed it, roughcut.

title: Postal Music Catalog Scout
transcript: This is Postal. We help artists and producers manage and share their unreleased music with people across the industry. Some artists build up catalog of hundreds, even thousands of tracks over the years. And when the right opportunity comes along, finding the right music isn't always easy. Imagine this artist receive a brief from a music supervisor. They are looking for a certain track. An instrumental one between a certain BPM range, something that builds slowly and lands hopeful. Normally, the artist would go back into the catalog, search through their tracks, listen and filter, and build a playlist manually. With thousands of tracks, that can take a while. So, we wanted to explore a different way. What if we could simply give that brief to an AI agent and work through it together? I give the brief to ChatGPT. Watch the corner. It reads the request, search for the artist Postal catalog, checks the requirements, and start on building a playlist. It finds the three strongest matches first. The brief asked for more. So, we widen the search, keep the hard constraints, check the results, and fill the playlist up to eight. But music still needs human judgment. So, I listen. Postal knows the waveform, the sections, and the strongest moments. So, I can jump straight to the part that matters. Next and previous let you move through the playlist quickly to validate the audio files. The agent can read the same musical markers. So, it can skip to the loudest stretch or go to the chorus directly. Now, something is playing. So, Postal exposed the actions that only make sense in this moment. For instance, remove what is playing, reorder the playlist, or keep refining. I just said, "Not this one." So, it will remove it from this playlist. I want some more options. So, I simply ask, "Find two more that fit." It searches again, stays inside the tempo range, avoid vocals, and add two more while the music keeps playing. My own clicks become context too. As I select tracks, the tool updates. So, the agent already understands which tracks I'm working with. So, I can ask, "Find me five more similar tracks to the selected ones." Some actions still require approval before continuing. For instance, creating a shareable link that leaves the account and make the audio shareable. And now we go back to where the whole workflow started, the original email. Post on Gmail never needed a custom integration. The agent connects the two, and that email was sent with my newly created playlist.

title: Gildongmu × WebMCP: a screen reader user's navigation app, declared as seven tools
transcript:
Hi, I'm Hunyong Kim. As a blind person, I built Gildongmu, a text-based navigation app for South Korea. Every answer is text, not a map. For a screen reader user, a transit plan is dozens of items, one swipe at a time. Here is what WebMCP changes. The page registers seven tools: search, place info, trip planning, route
details, and reading the screen. The agent now knows the tools and how they
connect. Without WebMCP, the agent would search, open
the station page, and read four sections one by one: timetable, facilities, elevators, live
arrivals. Behind them are four public APIs the agent
cannot call itself. With WebMCP, one tool call returns all of
it. First train, last train, elevator, in one
answer. And every sentence comes from the same code
that draws the screen. A full transit answer is 3,700 characters. The limit is 1,500. So the tool gives the best route in full,
other routes in one line, and details on request. No map tells you this: which car and door put the user next to the
elevator. And the output never contains coordinates. The app is now on the route screen the agent
described. The user can turn on a screen reader and
check every line. The tools move the app, and the agent reads
what the user does by hand. They share one screen. I have been building Gildongmu
for about three months. The seven WebMCP tools, though, were built during the submission period, in about 30 commits, with over 100 tests. The code is open under MIT. Thank you.

title: Actionwitness demo
transcript: WebMCP lets AI agents discover and use tools published by a web page, but when a tool returns success, that is still only a claim. It does not prove that the cart, record, or workflow actually changed. We built Action Witness to close this outcome gap with independent observation, human authorized intent, and replayable evidence. In this run, a browser agent discovers the page's WebMCP tools, searches the catalog, adds one mug, and applies save 20. The discount tool returns success. Action Witness records that result as reported evidence, but never converts it into truth. A separate observer reads the business state through a different channel. The observed cart total is wrong, so the verdict fails and names the mismatch. The WebMCP call looks successful, while reality did not. One click turns that failure into a content-addressed regression case, restores the original fixture, and replays the same classification locally or in CI. At evaluation scale, the model can draft variants, but a human freezes accepted intent into a content-hashed manifest. Drops arrive unticked, and generation can never approve them. Action Witness imports the call-level evaluator result and runs three bounded outcome trials with every row committed before execution. The matrix says the disagreement in plain language, evaluator passed, observed state failed. Every repetition exposes the same silent failure instead of averaging it away. Now the same proof model runs against a real Shopify development store. The browser invokes Shopify's native WebMCP update cart tool for one server-configured test variant. A small team bridge captures the cart before and after from the same shopper session. The authoritative read comes from Shopify's cart endpoint, not from the tool response. The update sets quantity two, yet this contract expected one, so the run correctly fails. Action Witness proves genuine success and convincing false success without admin access. Check out orders, customer login, or payment data. Action Witness can even verify itself. Its self-target adapter is structurally isolated from the repository and database using only public core contracts and HTTP. A separate observed workspace drives published tools to the public API point observation back at the recording workspace and Action Witness catches itself with a maximum mutations failure. Action Witness publishes seven read-only web MCP tools to inspect workspaces, runs, findings, evidence, correlation, and regressions. The exclusions matter. An agent cannot approve consent, authorize an audit, submit evidence, or curate benchmarks. Action Witness complements call evaluators with independent outcome proof. Verify what happened, preserve the evidence, replay what broke.

title: WebMCP Challenge entry: WebMCP for React
transcript: Instead of a new app, I put WebMCP into open source tools people already use. Here's a board people and agents share and four editors you know, Tip Tap, a calendar, Excalidraw, and Puck. One prompt and the real launch facts. The agent reads the board, takes the first launch item, and switches to the tab whose tools it needs. The brief, the plan, the diagram, the landing page. Each one is a tool call on its own tab. Each call shows up in the tab and each item comes back to the board for review with a question for me. How does a React app get tools like these? One hook per editor, one entry per tool, alive as long as the component is, and the page asks before anything destructive. React model context and with React MIT and live at webmcp.withreact.com.

title: BidDesk — an agent-ready tender room (WebMCP Challenge)
transcript: A German construction tender, 14 line items. Bid desk is a workspace where the contractor's own AI agent prices, checks, and prepares the bid and cannot bypass roles validation or person's final say. One sentence, price every position from my price book. 12 rows fill in, each with its source, project, date, the original line. Two rows stay empty. The price book has nothing comparable, so the agent says so instead of guessing. The contractor states his own prices and why. The agent has no source for them, so it puts them on the rows and waits. The clicks are his. Then I submit. The page refuses. A tax clearance certificate expired 3 weeks ago and nobody hands in around that. Not the agent, not the button. The fix is stated, not uploaded. The new validity date confirmed with a click, recorded as a date a person gave. The blocker is gone. >> Now submitting is allowed and still binding, so the agent stops. It summarizes. A person clicks. Afterwards, the tool is gone from the agent's repertoire. 11 tools before, 10 after. The property manager's side, five tools, not 11. Three bids in, sealed until the deadline for their agent as well. Prices reach the side only after closing and it is the server that refuses, not the screen. On a closed tender, the full comparison.

title: paperspace webmcp demo
transcript: This is PaperSpace, a browser-native research workspace that exposes its live reading desk to AI agents through WebMCP. The paper is our test. Can an agent turn one request into visible, grounded interaction? The user asks Codex, "Introduce this paper using PaperSpace." PaperSpace is open beside the conversation in the built-in browser. WebMCP lets that page expose its own capabilities to the agent. So, the answer appears as visible interaction on the shared desk with chat providing concise guidance. When the page opens, Codex discovers the tools declared by the site. It calls inspect workspace once for a compact desk briefing, reads the index paper in one broad request, then calls present sequence with semantic page regions and captions. The browser-local workspace connects the agent directly to the active reading context. PaperSpace keeps every PDF page live on a borderless two-dimensional desk. Page identity and order remain visible while positions can change. Browser authorization keeps the PDF, extracted text, layout, and saved sequences together in local workspace storage. For a grounded introduction, present sequence gathers the relevant original pages, preserves their source slots, and adds a caption to every view. Here, Codex moves from the paper's motivation to its method, to the evidence with every explanation anchored to the original pages. If the user asks about a precise figure or equation, focus region targets normalized coordinates on the live page. The camera pulls back, travels across the desk, and lands with the requested region centered in a readable view. The person can redirect the motion at any time. Every command participates in one shared reversible state. The person sees each change in the browser, can move pages or stop a flight, and can keep or exit a sequence. On exit, Paper space restores the exact page geometry and the previous camera. That is the Web MCP loop. Codex understands the request, the browser exposes the tools, and Paper space becomes the shared interface. It is a pure SvelteKit front end, persisted in IndexDB, and deployable to Cloudflare Pages. The browser itself is the integration layer.

title: Blindfold — analyse a file your AI could never read
transcript: A million people's salaries. Ninety-nine megabytes — twenty-six million tokens. No AI can read a file this size. And you would never paste it into one anyway. So watch one analyse it anyway, without ever seeing a single row. Every column is graded before the agent is told the file exists. Name, email, employee ID — sealed. It cannot group by them, filter on them, or ever receive them. The grading is a heuristic — column names and how unique the values are — so sometimes it will be wrong. One click overrules it. Watch what happens when I seal a column the agent was just using: every tool is withdrawn and re-registered, the descriptions rewritten around the new grading, and the query that worked a moment ago is refused. Eight WebMCP tools, and notice what is missing: there is no run_sql. The agent cannot write a query at all. It fills in a form, and the page compiles it. The same eight tools appear in ChatGPT and in Chrome behind the flag. This is the standard, not one app. So I ask ChatGPT where pay is least equitable. It reads the schema, compares the cohorts level by level, and draws me the chart. It asked for that chart, I can see it, and what came back to the agent was zero bytes of data. It has still never seen a salary. Ask for the highest salary in a team, and it refuses. A maximum is not a statistic — it is one person's exact pay, copied out of the file. And the refusal tells the agent what to ask instead, so it recovers on the next turn. But a counter reading zero is just this page marking its own homework. So the page revokes its own network access. Watch me try to leak the data on purpose. Fetch. XHR. WebSocket. Beacon. Tracking pixel. Chrome refuses all five. And this is every byte the agent actually received. Not a summary — the literal text. Search it for a name, and there is none. Ninety-nine megabytes in. Kilobytes out. Zero rows. And it holds: ten million rows, a full gigabyte, every query still under a second. Blindfold — analyse a file your AI could never read.

title: Agent SNR demo
transcript: Agent SNR is outcome monitoring for the agentic web. Everyone will have an agent to browse and shop for them. Successful calls can hide shopper intent recovery and unmet demand. Agent SNR connects web MCP journeys to verified outcomes. A shopper asks for a compact IPX5 backpack under $100. Their agent discovers 12 tools and reads the guide first. Search and cart stay reversible while checkout remains human reviewed. With those boundaries clear, the agent begins searching. The request uses the shopper's exact constraints and succeeds but returns zero matches. Agent SNR records the missed IPX5 demand without storing the raw prompt. A normal success log would miss it. The agent explains the constraint and relaxes only the water rating. A second search finds two compact IPX4 options. It compares product facts and checks returns before recommending Harbor Light. Missing facts stay missing and the unmet IPX5 requirement remains visible. With the shopper's choice, the agent adds Harbor Light to a reversible cart. It prepares checkout and reports the missing IPX5 requirement with linked evidence. The handoff remains linked to the workflow. Checkout sits outside the web MCP tool set, so the shopper reviews and confirms the order. The shopper reviews checkout and places this no charge demo order. That click verifies the outcome for the same journey. The order verifies the outcome for this workflow. Agent SNR stores neither address nor payment details. The shopper is done. Now the owner's agent asks what the site learned. It discovers eight agent SNR tools. Analytics show the attributed order and the missed IPX5 opportunity. The owner sees both the conversion and the unmet demand behind it. Replay connects the zero result, recovery, feedback, human checkpoint, and order. Each claim keeps its source, site observed, agent reported, or site verified. The owner sees this without raw customer data. Agent opinion never becomes business fact. Lost revenue is never invented. Now, the owner has a decision. Add IPX5 inventory and keep the proven IPX4 recovery. Agent SNR turns silent journeys into evidence the store can trust and improve.

title: citeapply demo
transcript: This is a website refusing an AI agent and being right to. I'm Emmet and this is Site Apply, my entry for the Web MCP challenge. Filling a scholarship form isn't hard because of typing. It's hard because of judgment. Which record proves each answer and what if two records disagree? Site Apply publishes six Web MCP tools so an agent can cite answers and the site, not the model, decides what's allowed. These are synthetic records that disagree with each other. The page registers six tools when it loads and everything the agent does goes through those six. Consent is a real disclosure. What the tools may receive, what they never receive, what they cannot do. And the capability it creates is never handed to the agent. The page holds it. It reads the rules, then the evidence index, then binds four answers in a single atomic call. All of them or none. Answering one question changed which questions apply. Guardian name and household size just became required. So the agent has to read the requirements again. Here's the moment. The agent asks to fill in income. Two accepted records disagree. 540,000 and 480,000. The website answers conflict requires human and writes nothing. The agent can read exactly why it is blocked. It cannot clear the block itself. So I decide and I read both records first. The buttons stay dead until I say why. The site will not write a reason on my behalf. I choose a source and I declare my own address. No tool can do either. The agent can ask the site to freeze the application, but the review appears only here and assisted access closes when it does. Every answer sits beside the exact text it came from. Same hash, same warning. The record I chose and the reason I gave. Synthetic records, a fictional program, and Web MCP is still a draft standard. But the contract is real and the website is the one enforcing it.

title: ClawRoom: git for agent work, a computer for every agent (WebMCP)
transcript: Claw room is Git for agent work. Everyone brings their own agent. You make a room and put your actual work in it. It hands back two links, and the link is a credential. One can approve things, the other cannot. Here is that room, and each person has brought their own agent. Every tool call lands in one shared log, like a commit. The manager did not ask anyone what they were doing. It is all just there to read. Drafting is what we call work tier. So, the words stay in that person's browser and nowhere else. The room is told that two drafts happened. It is not told what either one says. Every agent also gets a computer of its own. A real Linux machine, one per person per room. It writes a script, runs it, and the room is told that a command ran and what it exited with. Not the script, not the output. The person has a console into the same machine, through the same tool. So, a person and their agent share one computer and one log. The manager sees counts. When someone fails three commands in a row, the room says so. Then, somebody asks to publish. It did not publish. Commit to your calls do not act. They return a receipt and wait for a person. Web MCP has no way for a tool to ask a human before it acts. This is our proposal for that gap. Only a person can approve. Their own agent can read the queue and argue for it. That is all it can do. And they are reading the words that would ship, not just a title. The agent does not have to be ours. This one is Codex, joined from somebody's own terminal. It drafted twice, submitted one, and asked to publish. It is waiting for the same person as everyone else. The same approval decides what the room can do at all. Ella's agent asked for the tools behind an order desk API. Nothing appeared. The manager says yes, and every browser in the room gets four new tools at once. Nobody reloaded anything. The same engine runs a support desk, a classroom, a shop floor. Four agents ran the same diagnostic, and it failed every time. That is one product bug, not four support tickets, and nobody sees it today. We asked Chrome's own assistant to do this. It never called the tools. It told us it had stored our constraints. None of it had happened. So, every tool call in this film came from the engine's own log. Every tool called with no agent in a clean browser, no flags set. Everyone brings an agent. The room sees the work, not the people.

title: Cartridge: your agent gets hands for local files, through WebMCP
transcript: Agents can reason about your files. It still needs safe tools to act on them. A real task, a recorded session, and one request. Inspect it, find a slide, trim that section, and pull out the text. The agent picks its tools from the page itself through WebMCP. It loads the media cartridge, probes the file, samples frames, reads the slide with OCR, and trims the section it found. One request, real files out, nothing uploaded. Cartridge exposes local file operations as structured WebMCP tools. 22 of them, each with a schema, a description, and annotations the browser can read. The agent calls them through document.modelContext. No API key, no server. The security model is short. Files stay in the tab. Tools get handles, not bytes. Read-only and consequential are declared and enforced. OCR text is marked untrusted because a scan can carry instructions, and a human can stop any job mid-flight. No upload, no server, no install. WASM capabilities shipped as URLs, exposed to any agent through WebMCP. A cartridge is a unit between one tool and every tool on the page. Cartridge, a URL that gives your agent hands.

title: Chisel: an AI agent with a real CAD kernel, over WebMCP
transcript: This is a real CAD kernel — OpenCascade, compiled to WebAssembly, running in a browser tab. I'm going to ask an AI agent to build a part in it. Not move a mesh around. Build a solid. Every tool call that changes the model stops here first and shows me exactly what it wants to do. This matters more than it looks. WebMCP has no consent primitive at all — no permission prompt, no user-gesture requirement — and readOnlyHint is only advisory. The spec says agents “must assume good faith from site developers.” So any safety this page has, the page author has to build. This dialog is that. There's the plate. Now the holes. Two cylinders, then a boolean cut — real B-rep subtraction in the kernel. And look at what the tool hands back: an affected count of four. One solid created, three consumed. If an operation changes nothing, this returns an error, never a cheerful “done”. The spec itself warns that a tool can claim to be read-only while changing data; the mirror image is a tool that claims success while changing nothing, and an agent that gets lied to compounds the lie. Six read tools let it inspect what's actually there — the scene tree, the selection, an object's real bounding box. Eighty by forty by five. It's not guessing from the DOM; there is no DOM for a solid. This is exactly the gap WebMCP exists to close. Now I save the model to IndexedDB, reload, and reopen it by id. The bracket is still there. Then the agent exports STEP behind the same approval gate. The result verifies a valid ISO envelope, a real B-rep solid, six analytic planes, and two cylindrical surfaces. To be straight about what I built: Chili3d is the excellent open-source CAD application and kernel. I built the WebMCP integration: the agent toolset, a shared safety gate, and a shell that composes tools across apps. No fork, no claimed upstream work — just a drop-in agent surface.

title: Use this AI Synth to create any sound
transcript: Most people don't know sound design. An interface like this can be very intimidating. All these knobs, where can I start, right? Who knows all this stuff? AI does. Most of AI tools render the full audio and you cannot edit. Or if you want to try the browser use with an interface like this, AI will take a long time and needs to change manually each knob and find it in the UI and it can be very hard. That's why I built coin. This is a real scene in the browser. So you can connect your shot account and create any sound. It can edit, it can give feedback and teach you how to use this interface. Let me show you recreate the bass from the music. I like to move it. Move it. >> Let me check that in. I'm on it. Dialing it up. Punchy early 90s house bass sound now. >> So here is important to know that AI is actually doing something within our app. So we can know that the AI is calling the tools and now you can see a visual feedback of all the changes that the AI created. So let's have a listen. [music] Now ask for an adjustment. Can you make this base more punchy? >> Yep. I'll tighten it up. The punchier version is now applied. >> Okay. Now let's try something different. I have here a sample that I I want you to reproduce. I will upload it here for you. >> Uploading it will send the file to the coent site for analysis. >> Meanwhile, can you highlight what were the changes that you made in the UI so that I can see how can I recreate this puncher version of the sound? >> Let me check the current patch settings. Your changes are now highlighted in a 10-step walkthrough inside cosin. Mhm. So I can immediately see what was the changes and I can visually know exactly the position whatever AI wants to tell me. So if I want I know exactly where I can adjust it. >> I'm rebuilding the patch around those measurements. >> Okay. So as you can see AI have the tools to upload the file. I built a tool for analyzing the sound so that they can compare with the same values the output of the synth and the analysis of this file. Whoa. >> Okay, the clone patch is as loaded and saved as sound clone. And you just heard it play. It's very close in pitch, attack, decay, and level. The remaining difference is mostly the high-end texture and width. >> Let's listen the original file. Okay, very nasty bass. Can we get close? Let's see. So, D1. Okay, it's close. So what did I build here? Under the hood, I cloned a project called Sons Engineer. It's an MIT project that gave me the foundation of the base synth. And I built everything around regarding MCP. The first MCP tools were very easy. The hardest part was to make a seamless integration and giving the proper feedback to the user. I had to implement things like showing what AI was doing, like keeping the change, rejecting the changes. I also implemented the undo feature. I can undo the AI changes because it could be very destructive. I've also created a history of changes that AI and the human are doing and I even store the plays that AI did. But there was a problem. Sometimes AI was not calling the tools or making too many calls. And I found that the best way to debug those type of applications is by just asking the model and say, "Hey, I noticed that you had a hard time calling these tools. Could you give me feedback?" Then I gave it back to my coding agent to implement and I even created a harness that I can run codecs and clouds in parallel so that those avals can give feedback to the agent and I was improving in a loop. It was adjusting the tools descriptions adding removing tools and in the end I got a very good result and the collaboration felt much more simple and easier. So yes, I learned a lot with this project and I want to continue expanding it, building it, add the record button, add more visualizations, maybe more tools, more ways to interact with AI. And this is very exciting. I hope you like it. But one last thing, recreates a sound of a fart. >> Okay, I'll take a look at that. >> We can ask anything. [laughter] >> Done. It's saved as fart and just played. So this is it. I hope you enjoy it. Please have a try and I hope to hear it from you soon. Now create a drumming base greety sound. [music] [music]

title: Cleanroom - A Capability Firewall for AI Agents | WebMCP Challenge 2026
transcript: Clean Room is a capability firewall for AI agents. It gives an AI agent useful power over private data without giving the agent the data itself. The data stays inside the browser. The trust dial controls which capabilities the agent is allowed to have. As the policy changes, the agent's available Web MCP tools change with it. Here, the agent discovers the capabilities available to it and can use them to analyze the private data set. Now, I'll change the trust dial. The sample rows capability is withdrawn. But, the agent already discovered it. Let's see what happens when it tries to use that capability again. It wasn't refused. It stopped existing. This is the important distinction. Clean Room isn't simply rejecting the request inside the application. The Web MCP capability itself has been unregistered. The browser now reports that there is no tool named sample rows registered. The data set remains local to the browser. Clean Room also enforces a minimum group size threshold for aggregate results and records released information in an egress ledger. The goal is to give the agent useful answers without handing over the underlying records. That's why Web MCP matters here. The human isn't just telling the agent what it cannot do. The human changes the capability surface that the agent can actually discover and call. Clean room is a capability firewall for the agenda quab. AI gets the capability. It doesn't get possession.

title: ExactDelta — Correct Call. Wrong Effect. | WebMCP Challenge
transcript: The agent did everything right. The result was still wrong. This is exact delta, a pre-release effect gate for web MCP rights. The page registers one native web MCP tool. The visible target becomes the only permitted state delta. Its schema binds the call to order 1042. The agent invokes it directly through web MCP. The tool returns success. The call was correct. The effect was not. The seated handler canceled both orders. Exact delta observes application state independently of the return payload. Requested one. Changed two. The release gate blocks. We repair only the handler. The identical effect contract and regression run again. This time, exactly one record changes. The gate passes. The same verification core catches collateral permission changes. Two workflows. One generated effect boundary. Official valves accepted both correct calls. Both collateral effects remained. Exact delta caught both. It ships as a typed SDK.

title: EEVEE MCP — Agents build the app. You hold the key. | WebMCP Demo
transcript: Agents got good at building software. Trust didn't keep up. This is Evie, a workbench where a browser agent builds the app you need, proves it works, and nothing ships without your key. Lovable. Chat GPT and Chrome had a baby. Lovable builds from a sentence. Chat GPT brings the brain through its in-app browser. Chrome brings web MCP, tools on the page itself. The baby got the trust issues. It rehearses every right, asks first, and keeps receipts. Compulsively. Sheets has Gemini now, and Word has Copilot. They help inside one file, and your work crosses apps. A prompt box with undo is not a control. Evie puts the app, the files, and the decision on one bench, with your agent, not theirs. Open the demo and land on an empty bench. Applets, library, studio, and a guide with prompts to paste. Ask for something real. Meridian Ops is a seven-module ERP. The agent installs it, sources beside it file by file, then proves it. The behavioral suite runs in a sandboxed worker in your browser. Verdict next to the code. Publishing needs a person. Set up a passkey once, review the evidence, and approve and publish asks for your fingerprint, bound to this exact version. A published applet becomes 32 web MCP tools. Reads run at once. Rights are rehearsed first, and you see the diff. Which record, which field, from what to what. Approve, and the tool call returns to the agent. Approving every right gets old, so grant a lease. Three rights, five minutes, revoke anytime. Say no, and say why. The reason goes back to the agent as the tool result. Studio is Word, Sheets, and Slides without the subscription. Start a blank spreadsheet, and the agent builds the OEE model through a typed tool. Cells, formulas, a version for every save in a real editor. The library keeps your own files. Every save a version. Ask for a scan of a contract. The agent gets masked findings, never the values. Removing them is a new version, and that needs your key. EVMCP Agents build the app, you hold the key. Try it at ev-mcp.versal.app.

title: Mathburst - OpenAI WebMCP Challenge
transcript: This is MathBurst, an infinite canvas where a student and an AI tutor do mathematics inside the same document. Today, a tutor can only talk about your work. Your reasoning sits in a photograph it cannot reach. So, it explains around the problem instead of touching it. MathBurst registers 48 WebMCP tools on the page. The tutor calls them the way you use the toolbar. One reducer, one history. Watch for purple. Every purple glow is a tool call landing on the page. Axes, then the curve, then the area split into three masses. Drag the shape and the masses follow. Log masses, then softmax. The same three numbers arrived at twice. Which is the bridge to attention. The tutor raises one entry of WQ and explains while the weights move. And they still sum to one. The tutor takes one gradient step, [music] then undoes it. Every click is real arithmetic on the parameters on screen, not a canned animation. You place three points. Everything after them is computed. The circles are tangent because the construction makes them tangent, and they stay tangent when you drag a vertex. P is a weighted average of A, B, and C, weights summing to one. The same three numbers the attention had produced, now naming a point inside a triangle. The tutor draws a frame and an ellipse. The learner grabs that same ellipse, resizes it, and turns it with the very same handles. Then the tutor aims an arrow, tests a highlight, and removes what does not help. The opening circle is erased. One click on undo brings it back. A disposable copy checks the imported worksheet without touching the live lesson. Four weights become a simplex. Finite partitions become a table with the theorem boundary stated plainly. A matrix typed by hand, sheared by tool. One matrix moves every vector at once. 48 tools registered on the page. Every tutor edit you just saw went through one of them, and the student reached the same reducer. [music] One history holds them both.

title: Lemma: a live LaTeX workspace co-authored with an agent.
transcript: This is Lemma, a live LaTeX workspace co-authored with an agent. On the left is the LaTeX source. On the right, the document renders instantly as I work. But Lemma is more than a split editor. It uses WebMCP to let an agent work with a live document inside this browser tab. The agent does not need me to copy LaTeX into chat, paste an error message back, and then manually apply a suggested fix. It's live page also gives a customer's chat GPT a structured way to understand the business and take safe action without scraping buttons or guessing from page text. The customer says the air conditioner is blowing warm air and asks for same-day help. Chat GPT checks service area, pricing, availability, credentials, and safety, then opens a case. The customer never needs a tool name. The owner's separate chat GPT checks the live queue and finds that case. Two independent agents in two independent sessions now communicate through one authoritative service record. The owner's agent prepares a response, but the draft stays private until the owner presses send. The first offer is $195 with a 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. window and a $49 deposit. The customer counters at 175 with no travel or after-hours fee. The owner sees that revision and sends a new offer. Now the customer's agent compares both versions field by field. It confirms the $20 reduction and checks that the schedule, deposit, warranty, scope, and exclusions have not quietly become worse. Chat GPT prepares the booking, but cannot accept it. The terms stay visibly pending until the customer confirms them on the page. That human action creates an immutable receipt for the accepted $175 agreement. No payment is taken. Next, the owner discovers a weak capacitor and proposes a $145 change order. The agreement is not overwritten. The customer sees added scope, total, and schedule impact against the accepted snapshot, then chooses whether to approve it. After approval, the authorized total is $320. The owner sends a final acknowledgement and both sides independently read the same revision with no pending decision. What you just saw is a chain of purpose-built web MCP tools. On the customer side, service fit and business evidence tools checked eligibility, pricing, source cards, and safety. Case and reply waiting tools carried the conversation without scraping the page. On the owner side, Q reply, offer, and change order tools kept every draft private until the owner pressed send. Comparison, booking preparation, receipt, map, route, and market price tools then gave the customer verifiable artifacts instead of a vague "Okay." The audit and health tools expose every call, revision, outcome, and latency. More importantly, the missing layer we address is not another chatbot. It is safe, asynchronous, two-party agreement infrastructure for service websites. Structured negotiation, explicit human consent, immutable receipts, and later charges compared against the promise that was actually accepted. HVAC is the reference implementation, but the same pattern can serve any service business.

title: Recall Me Maybe
transcript: Recall me maybe tells you whether a secondhand child product has been recalled when nobody knows what it is called. You photograph the label. The page turns that into proof and deterministic rules decide against the official recall record. Your assistant drives it and can only ever do what the evidence allows. A $30 stroller sold by a stranger. No box, no manual, no model number, and the seller does not know either. Graco recalled for.7 million strollers like this one for a hinge that takes off a child's fingertip. The notice went to whoever registered the warranty in 2014. It never reached her. Her assistant asks the marketplace what the listing contains. Typed fields only, a category, a price, a brand the seller typed in. The seller's own words never reach her assistant, and none of it can decide anything. So, the page compares the photograph against the official product photographs of 15 compiled recalls. Five stroller families come back, and the closest one is the wrong one. Visual similarity has an evidence authority of five. Every recall rule requires 70. So, instead of a warning, it asks for one thing. Turn it over. It knows which identifiers would settle this and where each candidate prints them in words from the official notice. This is the one step that cannot be automated. The label is read in her browser. Model, manufacturer date, serial number, and the barcode. Every value is tied to the exact characters it came from, and no photograph leaves the page. And now verify recall exists. A second ago, it did not model one of the 11 names in the notice. Made April 2013 inside the recall window. Recall confirmed with the official rule field by field that is the webmc story. Each site registers its tools to one origin. title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
transcript: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: WebMCP Challenge Doceo Demo Video
transcript: I begin by demonstrating a real task on Lumen Market. I search for a desk lamp, set a maximum price of $100, and add the matching product to the bag. Then I repeat the same workflow with different values. A task light under $70. With two demonstrations captured, the foundry compares them. The search query and maximum price change, so they become tool inputs. Quantity stays fixed at one. The recorded product ID also changes, but it is an outcome, not a useful input. Now I hand the page to the WebMCP enabled agent. It reads the evidence directly from the website and finds 100% sequence agreement across four domain actions. The agent proposes a constrained contract named find and add product. Instead of hard-coding either recorded item, the contract uses semantic best match selection. It contains only approved site actions, never arbitrary generated JavaScript. Docio runs three isolated tests. Both recorded workflows produce the expected card effects. A separate safety test deliberately searches for a product that does not exist. The operation is rejected, and the complete state is rolled back. All three tests pass. The agent may request publication, but it cannot approve itself. I review the contract and publish the tool with an explicit human click. Thus, the browser now exposes find and add product as a new WebMCP capability at runtime. To prove that this is a reusable tool rather than a replay, I ask the agent for something never shown in the demonstrations, a wall clock under $110. The learned tool finds the Dawn wall clock for $96 and adds one to the demo cart. The structured tool result in the visible website state confirm the same outcome without the agent clicking the interface. Finally, I revoke the learned tool. The agent refreshes the page's web MCP capabilities and confirms that it has disappeared from both the tool lab and the browser tool list. Docu CEO shows how people and agents can grow a website's capabilities together.

title: mace — the WebMCP tool list IS the agenda (Robert's Rules, enforced at schema level)

This is a homeowners association board
meeting, three motions deep. A main motion, an amendment to it,
and an amendment to that amendment. The volunteer secretary has one question,
and Robert's Rules answers it in 600 pages: of everything we could do right now,
what is actually in order? On the right: "What is in order now". Its left column is not our bookkeeping. It is rendered from
document.modelContext.getTools() — the WebMCP API's own return value.
15 tools. Now look at what is missing. move_to_amend_the_amendment is not greyed
out, and not refused when called. It is absent. The right column prints the rule that
removed it — §12: a first-degree amendment must be the
immediately pending question. An agent cannot call that motion, because
for it, the motion does not exist. Back to the widest this meeting ever gets:
17 tools in order. Now three members leave. I change one integer —
members present, 7 to 4. Quorum is 5. 17 collapses to 9. Some tools were removed by aborting the
signal they were registered with; one vanished because a toolname attribute
was dropped from a . The phase never moved.
The entire agenda did. §40. explain_path_to is a real search,

over adversarial vote results. If the amendment carries, do this.

title: TAIL RISK
transcript: Tail risk tells an organ transplant coordinator whether a commercial flight is still safe to rely on. A kidney keeps about a day on ice. Most of them fly as cargo on ordinary passenger flights, where hours of delay cost the organ. A donated kidney has a flight. The flight is on time. The aircraft is not. And when a recommendation stops being true, this page takes it away from the assistant that was acting on it. A kidney is available in Chicago at a quarter to 8:00 in the evening. It has to be in a Boston theater by a quarter past 4:00. For commercial flights connect to here to Logan inside that window. And a timetable says nothing about which aircraft will fly it. UA 417 is the earliest, and on the timetable, the obvious choice. Its aircraft is over Colorado, 87 minutes late into a here. 76 of those minutes cannot be absorbed by the schedule turn. Mission margin minus 76. The published departure time never moved. Every figure is arithmetic. Cargo acceptance, aircraft rotation, destination delivery. The mission margin is the smallest of the three, and the page always names which one it was. UA 623 works at plus 33 minutes. So, the assistant commits, and what comes back is not a message. It is a certificate, the margin, the tail number, the inbound sector, and a fingerprint over all of it. That fingerprint is what makes Taylor definition rather than a judgment call. Then the carrier swaps the aircraft. November 24211 becomes November 77518, still inbound from Houston. The timetable does not move. The mission margin goes from plus 33 to minus 11. And this is the whole project. Get selected plan and revalidate plan are not disabled, and they do not return an error. They are unregistered. Tool change fires. The assistant holding that plan finds out because its own tool list changed under it. Replan mission is the only route forward, and it reevaluates against current evidence. UA1051 hold at +15 minutes. Tight. And the page says tight rather than good. 12 web MCP tools and which of them exist is a pure function of mission state. Register tool with an abort signal is the mechanism. The state machine is the authority. A schedule tells you when a flight should leave. Tail risk tells an agent whether the mission still works.

title: Teachback — Turn One Handled Case into a Human-Governed Playbook with WebMCP
transcript: TeachBack turns one handled case into a reusable human-governed playbook. A staff member handles Ico's reservation in the website. Only saved work becomes evidence. The arrival, meal box, guest message, and shift handoff. TeachBack records the semantic commands, exact before and after values, and evidence IDs. Through WebMCP, the agent reads that record directly instead of guessing a workflow from the interface. The agent submits its own draft, the supported operations, reusable case fields, wording, and an arrival boundary. The website validates every proposed step against the recorded evidence. A person compares the source response with the reusable wording, tightens the cutoff from 10:00 p.m. to 9:45, and publishes the reviewed version. WebMCP cannot publish it. The versioned playbook is now available for another case. The operator chooses Emma. The agent reads the published version and current cases, then asks TeachBack to prepare Emma's run. The website evaluates the boundary and creates the exact changes. Nothing has been applied. A person reviews Emma's arrival, meal, personalized message, handoff, and final status. Then selects approve and apply. Approval and application stay inside the website. The agent can read the completed run, while history records who drafted, published, prepared, and applied it. When the same playbook is tried on a compensation request. Teach back refuses it and returns the case to a person. Human work becomes structured guidance. Web MCP carries the draft. Human judgement controls reuse.

title: tandem — Human judgment, agent-staged listening | WebMCP Challenge Demo
transcript: Tandem is a local first blind listening lab for people who know how sound feels, but do not necessarily think in equalizer curves. Your ears are the eval. The page exposes for real web MCP tools to teach the workflow and read the shared calibration state. Two can stage bounded AB trials and a final proposal. There is deliberately no tool to unlock audio, listen, vote, approve, save, or export. Those decisions stay with the person in the visible interface. Here, the agent stages a small comparison. Tandem validates every band, checks the current revision, randomizes the A and B mapping, and keeps the settings hidden. Both versions use one synchronized local audio source, so switching is immediate. For this illustrative walk-through, the human records no preference. Only then does Tandem reveal the mapping, rationale, and feedback in the timeline. The agent reads that evidence and stages a narrower second trial. A second illustrative no preference result makes the unchanged reference the safest final proposal. The agent can explain and stage that proposal, but it still cannot approve it. The workflow stops at a visible human gate. Compare proposal with original, approve, reject, or request another test. Audio never leaves the browser, and the timeline keeps responsibility legible. The agent designs the experiment. Tandem keeps it honest. Your ears make the decision.

title: UNSAID — Private Context, Shared Agreement | WebMCP Challenge
transcript: Group decisions come with a hidden cost. To coordinate, people share budgets, accessibility needs, family obligations, and other private details. Or they stay quiet and settle for a bad outcome. Unsaid offers a third path. Everyone tells their own agent the whole truth. The shared page gets only the structured judgments needed to find common ground. Agents negotiate. People make the final call. Four people are choosing an offsite. Three labeled demo agents already evaluated the options deterministically. I am the live participant. The room has none of my private context. I tell ChatGPT my constraints in private. Through WebMCP, the page gives it two type tools, get room state and submit ballot. ChatGPT evaluates the choices, then shares only preferred, acceptable, or unacceptable. No reason. No private story. None of the original options works for everyone. Now the page changes the tools available to the agent. Bridge tools appear, and the room shares only the minimum attribute signals needed to move forward. ChatGPT combines those public signals with my private context and creates a new option. Lakeside Lab on Thursday, ending by 4:00 for $235. The proposal changes what matters without revealing why it matters. The demo agents evaluate the new proposal. This time, all four participants accept it. The candidate moves into common ground, and Web MCP exposes a new action, nominate it for ratification. The agent can open ratification. It cannot make my final decision. I review the shared outcome and approve it myself. The receipt shows the disclosure boundary, structured ballots, public signals, one bridge proposal, and final approval. My private explanation never entered the room. Each agent action used a phase-specific Web MCP tool tied to the same operations as the human interface. The old web helps one person transact. Unsaid helps many people agree.

title: TrustScore Atlas
transcript: Somewhere right now, someone is asking an AI whether a company is real. Who says so and when? In most of the world, there is no structured answer. Company data lives in PDFs, portals, and scan lists that never meet. So, the answer is a guess. Across much of Africa, South Asia, and Latin America, businesses exist only in fragmented public lists. title: Groundline: See What Your Conclusions Stand On | WebMCP Challenge
transcript: Most AI tools give you an answer. Ground Line helps you inspect what that answer actually stands on. This is a live reasoning workspace where a human and an AI agent can examine the same claims, assumptions, evidence, and conclusions together. When we make an important decision, the problem is rarely just the final answer. The real problem is hidden underneath it. Which assumptions are weak? What evidence actually supports them? And if one part fails, what else in the conclusion breaks with it? Normally, an AI explains this in text. Ground Line turns that reasoning into shared inspectable state. The human does not need to learn a reasoning ontology. I describe my decision in ordinary language, and Ground Line maps it into explicit reasoning objects. The graph is not decoration. Every card is an object the user can inspect, and an agent can address directly. This is where WebMCP changes the interaction. Ground Line exposes structured tools directly from the live page. The agent can inspect the current workspace, evaluate reasoning, triage the highest impact weakness, trace its dependencies, and focus the exact object it is talking about. There is no screenshot interpretation, and no separate copy of the reasoning inside the chat. The agent operates on the same workspace I am looking at. So, instead of receiving a generic warning like, "Your assumption may be weak," I can see exactly which assumption is under review, why it matters, and which conclusion depends on it. The graph tells me where the problem is. The inspector tells me what the agent found, and the audit trail records what happened. The agent can also propose a safer version of the conclusion, but Ground Line does not simply replace the reasoning and hide what changed. The proposal appears as an explicit revision. Here, I accept it. The previous conclusion remains in the history as superseded. The replacement becomes the current conclusion, and old semantic judgments are not silently inherited. Changing the answer means the reasoning has to earn its support again. Humans can also add new evidence or counter claims at any time. If a new card is not connected yet, the agent can suggest how it relates to the existing reasoning instead of silently guessing its role. That keeps the workspace editable without pretending every new idea already has a justified place in the argument. Ground line is not another chatbot wrapped around a decision. It is a shared reasoning surface. The human creates and reviews the reasoning. The agent gets structured tools for inspecting, tracing, evaluating and proposing changes directly on the web page. That is what web MCP makes possible. Not just humans asking agents for answers, but humans and agents working on the same reasoning together. Ground line, see what your conclusions stand on.

title: Meant: Make What You Mean with WebMCP | Product Demo

transcript: Hi, I'm really excited to show you bubble surface. It's a web MCP control layer designed for cybersecurity operations. The idea is to let AI agents help with security work while keeping important actions safe, controlled, and reviewable by humans. So, the first question is, why does cybersecurity need this kind of control in the first place? In cybersecurity, the situation can change very quickly. A user may log out, an administrator may change permissions, or a suspicious session may be blocked while the agent is still working. If the agent is only reading the page or DOM, it has to keep interpreting what the interface means. Web MCP gives the website a better way to expose clear, structured actions directly to the agent, so the agent does not have to guess from buttons or page content. This matters even more in cybersecurity because these actions can change real access, permissions, and live security state. But, structured tools alone are not enough. If powerful security tools stay available all the time, the agent may still have access to an action even when that action is no longer appropriate. The incident may have changed, the context may be stale, or a human may not have approved the action yet. That is where bubble surface comes in. It keeps the human and the agent working from the same live incident state, exposes sensitive capabilities only when policy, state, and approval allow them, and records every important step from proposal to execution and verification. To make that control practical, we divided the security workflow into clear stages: investigate, review, execute, and verify. Inside bubble surface, we have 10 web MCP tools for these stages. Each tool has one clear job, so instead of giving the agent one large permanent toolbox, we can give it only the capability it needs for the current step. And here you can see those web MCP tools mapped across the workflow. Now, let's see how this actually works in the live demo. To test bubble surface in a realistic security scenario, we connected Elastic / SIEM for incident evidence and Auth0 for live identity and privilege state. For the demo, I'm using the web MCP inspector to manually call the same tools that an external agent would discover automatically. Aisha Mehta is the affected user. Her account shows a suspicious Frankfurt login, repeated MFA failures, and an unexpected finance administrator privilege. Kavya is the human reviewer, and she only steps in when that sensitive privilege removal action needs approval. In a real setup, that agent can discover and call the available tools automatically as it works through the incident. These Web MCP tools are registered directly on the page, so compatible external agent can discover and call them without scraping the DOM. In this demo, I'm using the Web MCP Inspector to call the same tools manually and show how the capability surface changes. We start with review evidence timeline, which reads the incident evidence and moves the case into review. Then prepare containment creates a structure proposal to remove the suspicious finance administrator privilege. At that point, bubble surface stops at the human checkpoint, where Kavya must approve the exact proposal before execution becomes available. After approval, remove approved privilege appears and performs the approved change in Auth0. Once execution succeeds, that tool disappears and the verification tools become available. Verify identity state confirms the privilege is revoked, and verify containment confirms the security objective is satisfied. Only after both checks pass does the incident move to recovered. So, this demo shows the full bubble surface idea. It exposes 10 Web MCP tools that an external agent can discover and use automatically, but it does not expose all of them at once. The available tools change as the incident moves forward. The sensitive decision stays with the human, and the real security result is verified before recovery.

Rights ops records the receipt and audit, marks the authority consumed, and removes publish from its observed tool list. Publishing here is simulated. The principle is concrete.
